title: How the Census Shapes Politics: Send Us Your Questions
author: Ask Bolts
content:
News broke this month that the Trump administration is working on a plan to
order the Census Bureau to [exclude undocumented people in
2030](https://www.wired.com/story/census-proposal-would-stop-counting-
undocumented-immigrants-and-ignore-race-and-sexual-orientation/), a move
President Trump already pushed for ahead of 2020 as a way to skew
redistricting and subtract congressional seats from states with large
immigrant populations.

The push is yet another reminder of how the decennial census matters to
politics. In preparing for it, public officials make countless decisions on
what they’ll measure, and how. Where do they count college students or
incarcerated people, for instance—at their dorms and prisons, or at their
prior address? Do they ask about citizenship, which may scare many people from
participating?

By shaping the results, these choices also affect political representation.
Census data is used to apportion congressional seats, guide redistricting, and
steer government funding.

In her new book [“Data Are Made, Not
Found,”](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/D/bo277581183.html)
danah boyd, an ethnographer and professor of communication at Cornell, unpacks
how this pivotal civic exercise shapes our democracy.

In the runup to the 2020 census, she interviewed hundreds of civil servants as
they dealt with budget constraints and the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it
much harder for census workers to conduct their usual face-to-face interviews
and collaborate with community organizers.

Boyd has now agreed to answer questions from _Bolts_ readers about what she
learned while writing her book—what it takes to conduct the census, and how it
influences politics.

So, we want to hear from you. What do you want to know about the census’ inner
workings and why it matters to representation?

Are you curious about how the census shapes redistricting and the distribution
of power? Have you wondered how public officials seek to influence it or civil
servants prepare for it?

Let us know what’s on your mind, and boyd will respond to many of your queries
as part of our series “Ask Bolts.”

Share your questions with us in the form below by **Friday, August 28**. And
remember: all questions are welcome. Nothing is too in the weeds for _Bolts_!
